title: Elements
subtitle: All 118, by atomic number
about: The 118 chemical elements by atomic number, each with its category, period and one verified fact, usually the story behind its name.

cards.note: Henry Cavendish recognised it as a distinct substance in 1766; its name means 'water-former', because burning it produces water.
First detected in 1868 as an unexplained yellow line in the Sun's spectrum during an eclipse; Ramsay found it on Earth in 1895.
From Greek lithos, stone: Arfwedson found it in 1817 in the mineral petalite, whereas potassium had first come from plant ashes.
Named after the mineral beryl; the sweet taste of its compounds gave it the rival name glucinium, used until IUPAC settled matters in 1949.
Named from borax, a word traced to Arabic buraq; Humphry Davy, and separately Gay-Lussac and Thénard, isolated it in 1808.
From Latin carbo, charcoal. Its football-shaped C60 molecule, buckminsterfullerene, honours Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes share its structure.
Daniel Rutherford isolated it in 1772 as 'noxious air'; Lavoisier called it azote, 'no life', because animals suffocated in it.
Lavoisier named it 'acid-former', mistakenly believing all acids contain it; Scheele and Priestley had each isolated it independently in the 1770s.
Several nineteenth century 'fluorine martyrs' were injured or killed trying to isolate it, before Henri Moissan succeeded by electrolysis in 1886.
Ramsay and Travers found it in 1898 in evaporating liquid air; Ramsay's son suggested novum, 'new', rendered in Greek as neon.
Humphry Davy isolated it in 1807 by electrolysing caustic soda; the symbol Na comes from the Neo-Latin natrium.
Named after Magnesia, probably the district in Thessaly though possibly Magnesia ad Sipylum; magnetite and manganese share the same origin.
Humphry Davy proposed alumium in 1808, then aluminum in 1812; aluminium became the international standard, while North America kept aluminum.
Davy proposed silicium from Latin silex, flint; in 1817 Thomas Thomson changed the ending to -on, judging it a nonmetal like carbon.
Hennig Brand discovered it in 1669 by boiling down urine in search of the philosopher's stone; the name means 'light-bearer'.
Known since antiquity as brimstone, 'burning stone'; IUPAC adopted the spelling sulfur in 1990, and British institutions soon followed.
Scheele described it in 1774 but thought it an oxide; in 1810 Davy proved it an element, naming it from Greek chloros, pale green.
Rayleigh and Ramsay found it in 1894 after noticing that nitrogen from air was denser than nitrogen from chemicals; argos means lazy.
Davy isolated it in 1807 from molten potash using a voltaic pile, the first metal isolated by electrolysis; K comes from Latin kalium.
From Latin calx, lime, made by heating limestone; Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1808 by electrolysing its oxide.
Nilson found it in 1879 in Scandinavian minerals and named it after Scandinavia; Cleve then recognised it as Mendeleev's predicted eka-boron.
William Gregor found it in 1791 in black sand from a Cornish stream; Klaproth later named it after the Titans of Greek mythology.
Del Río found it in 1801 but was persuaded it was chromium; Sefström rediscovered it in 1830, naming it after the Norse goddess Vanadís.
From Greek chroma, colour, for its vivid compounds; Vauquelin isolated it in 1797 and detected it in rubies and emeralds.
Its name, like magnesium's, traces back to the Greek region of Magnesia; Johan Gottlieb Gahn is usually credited with first isolating it, in 1774.
Fusion in massive stars effectively ends near iron, whose nuclei are among the most tightly bound; the symbol Fe comes from Latin ferrum.
From German Kobold, goblin: miners blamed the spirits for ores that yielded no known metal and gave off poisonous fumes when smelted.
Miners called a copper-coloured ore Kupfernickel, blaming the sprite Nickel when it yielded no copper; Cronstedt extracted the new metal in 1751.
From Latin aes Cyprium, 'metal of Cyprus', where much Roman copper was mined; this became cuprum, hence the symbol Cu.
Probably named by Paracelsus after German Zinke, prong or tooth; Andreas Marggraf is credited with isolating the pure metal in 1746.
Lecoq de Boisbaudran named it after Gaul, his native France; critics claimed a hidden pun, since gallus means rooster, le coq, which he denied.
Mendeleev predicted it as eka-silicon, down to its density; Clemens Winkler found it in 1886 and named it after Germany, his homeland.
Called 'the inheritance powder' for its use in poisoning relatives, since its symptoms were vague; the Marsh test of the 1830s made detection reliable.
Berzelius discovered it in 1817 and named it after the Moon, Greek selene, because it resembled tellurium, already named after the Earth.
From Greek bromos, stench, for its pungent smell; it is one of only two elements liquid at standard conditions, alongside mercury.
From Greek kryptos, hidden; from 1960 to 1983 the metre was officially defined by the wavelength of a krypton-86 spectral line.
Bunsen and Kirchhoff discovered it in 1861 with the new technique of flame spectroscopy, naming it from Latin rubidus, deep red, after its spectral lines.
Named after Strontian, a Scottish village near which its mineral was found in 1790; it was recognised as new by its crimson flame.
Named after Ytterby, a Swedish village whose quarry produced the mineral that also gave names to terbium, erbium and ytterbium.
Named from the mineral zircon, related to Persian zargun, gold-like; its alloys clad nuclear fuel rods because they absorb few neutrons.
Named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, because it so closely resembles tantalum; Hatchett had first called it columbium in 1801.
From Greek molybdos, lead, because its ores were confused with lead ores and with graphite; Scheele showed it was a new element in 1778.
Greek technetos, artificial: the first predominantly artificial element, found in 1937 by Perrier and Segrè in molybdenum foil from Lawrence's cyclotron.
Karl Claus discovered it at Kazan University in 1844 and named it from Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia, in honour of his homeland.
William Hyde Wollaston discovered it in 1803, soon after palladium, naming it from Greek rhodon, rose, after the colour of one of its salts.
Wollaston discovered it in 1802 and named it after the newly found asteroid Pallas, itself named after an epithet of the goddess Athena.
The symbol Ag comes from Latin argentum, and Argentina takes its name from the metal; silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other metal.
Stromeyer found it in 1817 in impure zinc compounds sold by pharmacies; the name comes from cadmia, calamine, linked to the mythical Cadmus.
Reich and Richter discovered it spectroscopically in 1863, naming it after its indigo line; indium tin oxide makes flat-panel displays transparent yet conductive.
The symbol Sn comes from Latin stannum. Bending a bar of tin produces a crackling sound, the 'tin cry', caused by crystal twinning.
The symbol Sb comes from Latin stibium; powdered antimony compounds, often known by the Arabic name kohl, have been used as cosmetics since antiquity.
Müller von Reichenstein found it in Transylvanian gold ore in 1782; Klaproth named it in 1798 after Latin tellus, the Earth.
Bernard Courtois discovered it in 1811 in seaweed ash used to make saltpetre for gunpowder; Gay-Lussac named it from Greek for violet.
From Greek xenos, stranger; in 1962 Neil Bartlett made the first noble gas compound with it, overturning the belief that these gases were inert.
Bunsen and Kirchhoff found it in 1860 by its blue spectral lines; since 1967 the SI second has been defined by a caesium-133 hyperfine transition.
From Greek barys, heavy, after its dense mineral baryte; barium sulfate has been used since 1908 to make the digestive tract visible on X-rays.
From Greek lanthanein, to lie hidden: Mosander found it in 1839 concealed as an impurity in cerium nitrate. It gives the lanthanides their name.
Named by Berzelius after Ceres, discovered two years earlier and then considered a planet; cerium metal provides the sparks in ferrocerium lighter flints.
Greek for 'green twin': in 1885 Auer von Welsbach split didymium, long thought an element, into praseodymium and neodymium.
Greek for 'new twin', separated from didymium in 1885; neodymium iron boron magnets pack strong fields into headphones, hard drives and electric motors.
Named after Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods; Grace Mary Coryell, wife of one of its 1945 Oak Ridge discoverers, suggested it.
Named after the mineral samarskite, so the Russian mine official Samarsky-Bykhovets became the first person, albeit indirectly, to have an element named after him.
Demarçay isolated it in 1901 and named it after Europe; red-glowing security features on euro banknotes show europium's characteristic emission.
Named, via the mineral gadolinite, after Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin, who discovered yttrium's oxide; its paramagnetism makes gadolinium compounds useful MRI contrast agents.
Another Ytterby element; through nineteenth century confusion, the names terbium and erbium were switched, and they have stayed switched ever since.
From Greek dysprositos, hard to get: in 1886 Lecoq de Boisbaudran needed more than thirty attempts to separate it from holmium oxide.
Named from Holmia, Latin for Stockholm; having the highest magnetic saturation of any element, holmium forms pole pieces of the strongest static magnets.
Mosander found it in 1843 in yttria from Ytterby; erbium-doped optical fibres amplify the 1550 nanometre light carrying long-distance telecommunications.
Cleve named it in 1879 after Thule, an ancient name for a far northern land; its original symbol, Tu, was later changed to Tm.
The fourth element named after Ytterby; in 2013 a pair of ytterbium atomic clocks at NIST set a record for stability.
Urbain named it in 1907 after Lutetia, the Latin name for Paris; Auer von Welsbach's rival name, cassiopeium, survived in Germany until the 1950s.
Coster and Hevesy found it in Copenhagen, Latin Hafnia, in 1923, searching zirconium ores because Bohr's atomic theory suggested a resemblance to zirconium.
Ekeberg named it in 1802 after Tantalus, who could never drink the water around him, because the metal's oxide could not absorb acid when immersed.
Swedish tung sten means heavy stone; the symbol W comes from wolfram, still used in many languages. No element has a higher melting point.
Named after the Rhine by Noddack, Tacke and Berg in 1925; Masataka Ogawa had probably found it in 1908, but misidentified it as element 43.
Smithson Tennant named it in 1803 from Greek osme, smell, after its pungent volatile oxide; osmium is the densest stable element.
Named after Iris, goddess of the rainbow, for its colourful compounds; an iridium-rich clay layer inspired the theory that an impact killed the dinosaurs.
From Spanish platina, little silver; from 1889 to 1960 the metre was defined by the length of a platinum-iridium bar.
The symbol Au comes from Latin aurum; gold's yellow colour is thought to arise from relativistic effects on its electrons, a classic textbook example.
The symbol Hg comes from Greek hydrargyros, water-silver; in 1911 Kamerlingh Onnes discovered superconductivity in mercury cooled to about 4 kelvin.
William Crookes discovered it by flame spectroscopy in 1861, naming it from Greek thallos, green shoot, after its bright green spectral line.
The symbol Pb comes from Latin plumbum; lead is the stable element with the highest atomic number, and three isotopes end major decay chains.
Long thought stable, bismuth-209 was found in 2003 to undergo alpha decay, with a half-life about a billion times the age of the universe.
Marie and Pierre Curie discovered it in 1898 and named it after Poland, then partitioned, hoping to publicise its lack of independence.
From Greek astatos, unstable: Corson, MacKenzie and Segrè first made it at Berkeley in 1940, and all its isotopes are short-lived.
Rutherford and Owens discovered it at McGill in 1899 as an 'emanation'; Ramsay and Whytlaw-Gray later proposed niton, from Latin nitens, shining.
Marguerite Perey discovered it in 1939, the last element first found in nature rather than synthesised; it was the second named after France.
The Curies announced it in December 1898, naming it from Latin radius, ray; Marie Curie and Debierne first isolated the metal in 1910.
From Greek aktis, ray; Debierne named it in 1899, though the element itself was probably first truly obtained by Giesel in 1902.
Berzelius named a supposed element after Thor in 1815, but it proved to be yttrium phosphate; he reused the name for real thorium in 1828.
Fajans and Göhring first called it brevium in 1913; Meitner and Hahn renamed it protactinium, 'before actinium', the element it decays into.
Klaproth discovered it in 1789 and named it after the newly discovered planet Uranus; Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 using uranium.
McMillan and Abelson made it at Berkeley in 1940, the first transuranic element; Neptune is the next planet beyond Uranus, as neptunium follows uranium.
Named after Pluto, continuing the planetary sequence; Seaborg chose the symbol Pu as a joke, after 'P U', an exclamation at a bad smell.
Named after the Americas by analogy with europium, the lanthanide directly above it; americium powers the ionisation chamber in many household smoke detectors.
Named after Marie and Pierre Curie, following the example of gadolinium above it, named after Johan Gadolin; first made at Berkeley in 1944.
Named after Berkeley, California, where Seaborg, Ghiorso, Thompson and Street first made it in December 1949 using the 60-inch cyclotron.
First made at Berkeley in 1950 and named after the university and state of California; its neutron-emitting isotopes help start up nuclear reactors.
Named after Albert Einstein; first identified in fallout from Ivy Mike, the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952, and kept secret until 1955.
Named after Enrico Fermi; it is the heaviest element that can be made by bombarding lighter elements with neutrons, the route to macroscopic quantities.
Named after Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table; during the Cold War, Seaborg needed US government permission to honour a Russian.
Named after Alfred Nobel following a 1957 Swedish claim, soon retracted; in 1992 IUPAC credited a Soviet team but kept the familiar name.
Named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron; the Berkeley discoverers proposed the symbol Lw, but IUPAC changed it to Lr.
Named after New Zealand physicist Ernest Rutherford, father of nuclear physics; Soviet scientists claiming priority had called it kurchatovium instead.
Named after Dubna, home of Russia's Joint Institute for Nuclear Research; Berkeley had proposed hahnium, a dispute settled only in the 1990s.
Named after American chemist Glenn Seaborg; it is one of only two elements named after a person still living at the time of naming.
Named after Niels Bohr; the Darmstadt discoverers of 1981 proposed nielsbohrium, which IUPAC shortened to bohrium.
Named after the German state of Hesse, Latin Hassia, home of the GSI laboratory in Darmstadt, which first made it in 1984.
Named after Lise Meitner, a discoverer of nuclear fission; it is the only element named solely after a real, non-mythological woman.
Named after Darmstadt, the German city whose GSI laboratory, which also made elements 107 to 112, first created it on 9 November 1994.
Named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays; the Darmstadt team made it in December 1994, detecting just three nuclei.
Named after Copernicus on his 537th birthday in 2010; experiments suggest it is so volatile it may be a gas or liquid at room temperature.
Named after Nihon, Japan, where Kosuke Morita's team at Riken made it; it was the first element named by Asian physicists.
Named after Dubna's Flerov Laboratory and physicist Georgy Flyorov; the Cyrillic ё is transliterated as e, hence flerovium rather than flyorovium.
Named after the Moscow region, home of Dubna's Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, where a Russian and American team first made it in 2003.
Named after Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Dubna's partner; the first livermorium atom, a single one, was detected at Dubna in July 2000.
Named after Tennessee, where Oak Ridge produced the berkelium target; 2016 naming rules gave it the halogen ending -ine rather than -ium.
Named after Yuri Oganessian; though placed with the noble gases, relativistic effects are predicted to make it a reactive solid at room temperature.
